issues.item: Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma profile, 'Medical Procedures' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the report. The memory items describe classic reliving/terror reactions, and the formulation shows a strong Memory → Triggers link, implying triggers should plausibly cue the stalking memory. 'Loud noises' and possibly 'happy families' can occur idiosyncratically, but a medical examination trigger is clinically disconnected from stalking unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere. This makes the trigger set less coherent with the trauma type and formulation.

vignette:
Linh Nguyen is a 38-year-old stock broker who came to treatment after months of trying to keep her life narrowed to what felt manageable. She described the stalking as something that began quietly enough that, at first, she questioned whether she was imagining it. On her walk from the subway to her office in the financial district, she started noticing the same man behind her on different mornings. Then he began appearing outside her apartment building in the evenings, standing near the curb or across the street as if he were waiting for someone. What made the situation unmistakable to Linh was the way he started closing the distance between them. One night, as she reached her building entrance, she smelled alcohol before she saw him clearly. He was close behind her, speaking in a low voice she could not fully make out, and when she turned, she saw his face and the glassy, intoxicated look that told her he was drunk. She remembered the panic of fumbling for her keys while hearing him come nearer, the sharp slam of a car door somewhere on the street making her jolt so hard she nearly dropped everything. After that, the stalking no longer felt ambiguous. It felt immediate, physical, and dangerous.

In the weeks that followed, Linh reported that the memories did not stay in the past in any settled way. When she remembered what happened outside her building or the many times she caught sight of him trailing her, she did not experience it as a distant recollection. She said it felt as though it were happening right then, in the present, with the same surge of terror in her chest and the same certainty that she was about to be cornered. At other times, the opposite quality was what unsettled her most: the whole thing felt so extreme that she struggled to believe it had actually happened to her. She would find herself thinking that it sounded like something from a television drama or a story about someone else, not her life, not a woman whose days were usually organized around market openings, client calls, and the small routines she shared with her partner. That sense of unreality did not comfort her. It left her feeling unsteady, as if her own memory could not be trusted even while her body reacted with full force.

Her triggers became woven into ordinary life in ways that made the world feel unpredictable. On the trading floor, loud noises were unavoidable: a sudden shout across the room, a phone dropped hard onto a desk, the abrupt crack of something falling in the office kitchen. Each sound could send her instantly back into the physical alarm of those evenings when she had heard footsteps, doors slamming, or movement behind her and believed he was right there again. She found herself stiffening at work, scanning the room before she could return to the spreadsheet or conversation in front of her. The smell of alcohol was especially difficult. If a client came in after a lunch meeting with wine on his breath, or if she passed a bar on her way home and caught the stale scent of beer drifting out, she was no longer on the sidewalk in lower Manhattan; for a few moments she was back at her apartment entrance, keys in hand, with him close enough to smell.

What surprised Linh was one of the triggers she felt embarrassed to admit. Seeing happy families could shake her badly. A couple with children laughing over brunch, parents walking hand in hand with a stroller, even a polished advertisement showing an easy domestic life could bring on a sudden, disorienting sense that she was watching a world she had been shut out of. She had been in a relationship throughout the stalking, and her partner had tried to be supportive, but Linh found herself going blank or tense in moments that were supposed to feel warm and ordinary. A family scene would catch her off guard and she would feel a pang of distance, followed by the same terror that seemed to arrive from nowhere.

Over time, her world became more constricted. She adjusted commuting routes, lingered in the office until she thought the streets would be busier, and avoided after-work gatherings where alcohol would be prominent. Her job, once a place where she moved briskly and confidently, became another setting where she was bracing herself. Colleagues noticed that she startled easily and seemed distracted after sudden noise. At home, her partner grew increasingly concerned as Linh pulled away from simple shared plans and struggled to explain why a smell, a noise, or the sight of a cheerful family on a neighboring block could unravel her. What finally brought her to seek help was a recent episode outside her office when a delivery cart crashed loudly against a metal doorway just as she passed a man reeking of liquor. She froze, heart pounding, convinced for several seconds that the stalking was happening again. By the time she made it upstairs, she was shaken and ashamed, frightened by how quickly the present disappeared when something reminded her of it. She said she wants help because she cannot keep living as though danger is always about to step out from behind her, and because what frightens her most is not only the memory itself, but how completely it can take over her sense of what is happening now.
